_what: Settings of the computers rows (src/account/computers.rs). A computers row says which computers hold a copy of an account or of a pursuit and which of them may answer. It is the account's own row, kept in its sign-in rows (sign_in/families.json family `places`), signed with the account's own signing key (Ed25519), and the owner or the team edits it by one row edit with a revision compare-and-set. `signed_domain` is the first field of every signed row, so a signature made for another purpose never verifies here. `account_id_context` derives an account's address from its public key (BLAKE3 derive_key): credentials and the forwarder name an account by its address, so the address itself names the key that signs the account's rows and a forwarder can check a row with no stored state; the account's internal owner id is separate and never changed by it. `computer_id_context` derives a computer's own signing key from its computer key, and `proof_uses` names each use a computer signs for, with the domain it is signed under: `session` (it opens a session to a forwarder), `message` (one message it posts there; the forwarder hands a message's proof on to the computer it is for, so a message proof must never open a session), and `claim` (an email claim the sign-up sends the operator account, src/native_entry/computer/email_claim.rs), `key-check` (a computer's ask of the sign-in tool whether an api key it was shown is valid: the parts are the BLAKE3 hex of the key, src/account/computers/key-check-fixture.json is one signed example the sign-in tool's own check is tested against), and `lookup` (the root sign-in's ask of the operator account for the address an email goes by, src/native_entry/computer/email_address.rs; only a hosting computer's signed ask is answered with the address). A signature for one use never verifies as another; `computer_proof_window_ms` is how far that signed time may be from the forwarder's clock. `account_prefix` and `pursuit_prefix` start a computers row's id (one row per account, one per pursuit); `key_prefix` + the account's user id is the row that holds the account's public key. `signing_key_value` is the secret (src/secrets.rs) that keeps the account's signing key, sealed under the secrets key. `limits` are the limits read by name from an `access` the way old trillion's payment fold made it (src/payment.mjs:368-408: `access.limits` holds, by name, each active offer's `allowances` row less its `access`, and each active contract snapshot's `limits` row less its `key`): `computers` names how many computers one computers row of an account may name (copy keepers, and voters), read from the account's own `account_policy.access`; `accounts` names how many accounts one computer holds, read from the computer config's `access`. `shipped` are the default rows, old trillion's numbers (`max_computers` 16, `accounts_max` 256), which always count: a plan or contract row raises them and the most generous row wins (old trillion src/contract-entitlements.mjs `quantityFor`); no row is the shipped default, never unbounded. `row` bounds the account's limits row (src/account/computers/limits_row.rs, door ops `sign-in:limits` and `sign-in:set-limits`): its id starts with `prefix`, each source it holds is named by one of `source_kinds` and a name of at most `name_bytes` (a plan's offer, a contract's key), and gives at most `most_names` limits of at most `most_rows` rows each, each row at most `row_bytes` of JSON; the row holds at most `most_sources` sources; the rows of every source are added to the account's `account_policy.access` under the same names before a limit is read. `most_admitted_computers` is the hard admission bound (Local First Architecture §4.6): no row naming more computers is signed or believed, whatever its plan. `pursuit_id_bytes` bounds a pursuit's id. `max_told_rows` bounds the rows one computer tells when its session opens: a computer opens one session for itself that carries every account it holds (src/native_entry/computer.rs `keep_forwarder_sessions`), so it is the shipped `accounts` limit (256), and the accounts past it get a session each. `kept_accounts_max_bytes` bounds that list of kept accounts message. `operation_edits_max` bounds the edits one computers operation (src/account/computers.rs `apply`: add a computer, remove a computer, set the computer in use, move the writer, set the lists) tries: one per voter step, and one more each time another edit landed first and the operation is applied again to the row read then; before it is applied again it waits a random while below `operation_backoff_ms` doubled for each such edit in a row (up to 64 times), so two operations that keep undoing each other's voter steps do not both run out of edits. `this_computer` is the report this engine gives of the computer it runs as when the computer config names none: what it has, what it reaches, what it costs, whether it runs contained tools, whether it is on all the time (a report only, never required), whether it takes new accounts. The local ports it serves (`local_ports`: a name a tool row lists in `invoke.local_doors` and its loopback port) and the folders it keeps programs in (`program_folders`) are only what a computer reports about itself in its own config's `report`: this default names neither, so a computer with no report has no local ports and no program folders beyond the system's and each program's own `search_path` (a tool row's `invoke.programs`, or src/tool_runs/tools/tool-runs.json). The hosting app's own report is its launcher's (product settings section `hosting_app_report`, src/account_files/identity.json), which its start (src/native_entry.rs `run_selected`) chooses the same way a computer chooses its config's `report` (`choose_this_computer`). A computer says nothing else about itself. `this_computer_sign_in` is the sign-in values of the computer it runs as when no computer config names them (the hosting app, which has no computer config yet): the relying party labels, the request body limit and the expired rows one write deletes (src/account/sign_in.rs `ComputerSignIn`); a computer takes them from its config's `sign_in`. `storage` is the same budget shape the record store reads (`bytes` or `keep_free_bytes`, see src/storage/record_store/settings.json). `voters` are the computers the owner names to vote on the writer row (src/account/computers/writer_row.rs): a term moves only when more than half of them accept it. `writer_row_prefix` starts the writer row's id (one per account, one per pursuit). `term_ms` is how long a renewed lease lasts on a voter's clock; `renew_every_ms` is how often the holder renews it, only while the account is active: the writer term is taken on the account's first write (src/account/computers/copies.rs `write`), renewed only while requests (writes or reads) keep coming, and released once none came for `idle_release_ms` (`step_if_active`), so an account nobody uses holds no term and runs no timer; the next write claims it again; `clock_margin_ms` is the allowed clock skew between computers, and a holder stops writing `clock_margin_ms` before its term ends while a voter waits that long past the end before it accepts a takeover. Copies (src/account/computers/copies.rs): a write with voters named commits only once a second copy holds it; `ack_wait_ms` is how long it waits for that before it rolls back and gives the writer role up. `message_wait_ms` bounds one message from a computer to another through the forwarder. `feed_page_items` is the most changes one page of the writer's feed carries. `replicated_resources` are the records resources every copy follows from the start (more are learned as they are written). `message_operation` and `http_operation` name the messages the forwarder sends a computer on its session: a message from another computer, and an HTTP request for a path under `/a/<address>`; `answered_by_header` is the response header the forwarder adds to each answer of an HTTP request it carried for an account, naming the computer (its id) whose session answered it, so a person or a proof can tell which computer answered without its logs. A computer's own listener sets the same header, its own id, on every answer it gives (src/native_entry/computer.rs `Computer::app`), so a computer reached through another front (a reverse proxy) names itself too; the forwarder sets it last, over the computer's, with the computer whose session it used. An account's door alone (no listener) sets none. `message_path` is the path part, after `/a/<address>/`, a computer posts a message to the forwarder on; `message_body_bytes` bounds the body of one such request or answer of the writer's page feed (a page of changes, a history page, a sign-in page) and of the answer to an HTTP request for the account; the request itself is bounded by the door's one request limit (src/mcp/settings.json `request_bytes`) and crosses the session as one message. A settle of records (`Message::Settle`, src/storage/record_store/record_sync.rs) is bounded by the records store's own `settle.bytes` (src/storage/record_store/settings.json: old trillion's 4 MiB per message), and a message or an answer longer than `message_body_bytes` (one record alone, a settle up to `settle.bytes`) travels in parts (`Message::Part`, `Answer::Parts`, src/account/computers/copies.rs `send`), each part within `message_body_bytes`, up to `carried_bytes` for the whole: old trillion's bound on one carried row, which travelled as a page of its own (Trillion-X/trillion src/resource-state-carry.mjs:11 `ROW_BYTES`, 16 MiB). The forwarder passes on, and a computer reads an answer, up to `message_body_bytes`; the receiver keeps the parts of one message from each computer (and of one answer to each computer) for at most `part_hold_ms` before it forgets them. A message whose answer did not come back and that failed early (within half of `message_wait_ms`: a connection that broke, not a computer that is slow to answer) is sent again, at most `resend_when_lost` times (src/account/computers/copies.rs `send_on`): one lost message no longer makes a write, a sign-in change or a renewal fail, which made the writer give its place up (measured 2026-11-04: one post to the other computer that may answer failed after 125 ms about every 2 to 5 minutes, and each moved the writer). Every message between computers may be taken twice: a copy applies a page only on top of what it holds, a voter accepts the same renewal again. A write's wait for its acknowledgement (`ack_wait_ms`) grows by `part_wait_ms` for each part after the first of a message it sends in parts, so a large write is not refused for its size. A computer whose account's computers row changed while its session stays open posts the new row to `message_path` + `/` + `tell_again_path` (src/forwarder/gateway.rs), with its own proof, and the forwarder takes it for that computer's live session (src/forwarder/connected_computers.rs `tell_again`): the forwarder learns an edited row with no new session. A computer id is 64 hex, so `tell_again_path` never names a computer. What travels besides records (copies.rs, rows_copy.rs): `feed_history_items` is the most versions in between one change carries (none when one change with them does not fit `message_body_bytes`); a copy takes the rest of a record's history in pages of at most `feed_page_items` versions, each within `message_body_bytes`, before it takes the change. The account's own rows (every family of src/account/rows/families.json) travel to every computer the row lets answer (never to a computer that only holds a copy); rows of the `places` family whose id starts with `writer_row_prefix` or `copy_prefix` stay at their computer. Each change of such a row is kept in the computer's copy log (`copy_prefix` + family + `:` + id, family `places`), stamped from the counter row `copied_row`; `sign_in_page_items` is the most changes one sign-in page carries. A computer other than the writer admits a sign-in from its copy only for `admit_ms` after it last caught up with the writer (and never past the writer's own term), and a sign-in change at the writer is acknowledged only once every computer that may answer holds it or that time has run out at it. At a computer that is not the writer, every change of a copied row is refused. A computer's proof (`trp_`) carries its clock: a voter refuses a vote from a computer whose proof time is more than `clock_margin_ms` from its own clock, so that computer cannot claim or keep the writer row. While no writer is known (its term ran out at a voter, plus `clock_margin_ms`), a computer that may answer may admit from its copy for `vouch_ms` after it asked, when more than half of the voters vouch that it holds every sign-in change they hold (`Message::Vouch`); a voter vouches only while no term is live in its own writer row, keeps the time it gave, and tells it with every vote it answers, so the next writer counts that computer as one that may still admit until then. 0 turns vouching off. A row written in the account's folder outside its copies is made one acknowledged change of the account's rows when the computer that serves the folder takes it (src/account/computers/copies.rs `copy_outside_changes`).. `pending_writes.settle_max_age_ms` (600000) is how long a queued command waits before it completes as refused (its cause `settle_timed_out`). It is six times the longest legitimate wait for a writer: an idle account releases its turn after `idle_release_ms` (60000), a new claim waits up to `joining_retry_max_ms` (30000), and one claim backoff with its jitter (`claim_backoff_ms` 5000 + `claim_backoff_jitter_ms` 5000) passes first: 100000 ms. The factor six is a choice, not derived; it only has to outlast a takeover.
_why: revocation_settle_ms: a revocation is a write that settles by majority and reaches every copy. Until it settles, a copy may still admit a turned-off key; after this bound every copy refuses it. The window is DATA so the cut-off and revoke-at-A tests assert it.
account_id_context: trillion account id from its public key v1
computer_id_context: trillion place signing key from its place key v1

scope_classes._what: The scope classes a resource can declare (plan 4a, B-2): lease-writer takes one fenced order, granted by a majority of the voters; crdt-merge writes on any computer and merges by stamps; local is one computer's state. The writer row of a subject is keyed by its class: lease-writer keeps the row id it always had, every other class adds '#' + its name. An unknown class name is refused.

account_stores._what: The stores an account's routes open besides its records, vault and own rows (its policy directory and its app key-value entries with their blobs, src/account/create.rs `AccountStores`) travel as records of `resource` in the account's own records store, so the writer's feed carries every later change of them to every copy (src/account/computers/account_stores.rs). At the writer, each step (and each request it answered) writes the rows of its stores that differ from those records, at most `rows_per_write` rows per acknowledged write; at every other computer that may answer, the records are written back into its own stores once they changed. A row's record id is `policy_prefix` + its name or `kv_prefix` + its key. The policy names and key-value keys that start with one of `policy_kept_here` or `kv_kept_here` are each computer's own and never travel: the operator's service records are published by each computer into every account it serves (src/local_account/service_records.rs). A computer that only keeps a copy takes these records sealed, as every record, and makes no stores from them.

copy_rule._what: How many copies an account keeps (src/account/computers/copy_rule.rs). room_inodes is derived, not picked: 13408 = 13358 + 24 + 26. 13358 is one new shared commit tree (workshop-commits/<commit>, measured on hel1 2026-11-12: 10602 files and 2756 folders, counted with bytecode); 24 is one new account outside its Workshop folders (measured: 2213 entries over 91 accounts); 26 is the largest measured change in those account entries over 9 minutes (2213 to 2187). The multiplier is 1: a follower installs at most one newest commit per pass (install.rs install_commit), so one new tree is the most a pass needs before the next room check. The rule itself is the account's own list rows in its sign-in rows (family `lists`), made from the making computer's config `new_accounts` (`copies`, `copies_rules`): `copies_prefix` + the account's user id is its copies row ({revision, settings: {least_copy_keepers, least_voters, least_may_answer, least_always_on}}); `rules_prefix` + user id holds its formula field `short_by`, its trigger rule and its workflow definition; `offered_prefix` + user id is the account's offered-computers list (the computers it may add, each with what its report said); `run_prefix` + user id + ':' + run id is one workflow run. `list_name` is the name the computers row is shown under as a list (one row per computer). `change_kind` is the path the copies row is handed to the trigger rules under, `rule_partition` and `workflow_partition` the partitions the rules and runs are handed. `add_computer_ask` and `voter_step_ask` are the asks a workflow step makes that this file answers: the first adds the first offered computer with room as a copy keeper that may answer, the second makes that computer a voter once it reports caught up. `most_runs` bounds the runs one account keeps and `most_passes` the passes of one run in one call; `sweep_every_ms` is how often a computer re-reads short_by of every account it holds (old trillion src/keep-running.mjs: the hourly sweep); the rule also runs at once when the writer hears an added computer report it caught up. Every `report_every_ms` a computer posts its own report (always on, takes new accounts, has room) to its forwarder at `/a/<its id>/<message_path>/<report_path>` and hears back every report the forwarder holds of a computer whose own session is live, with when it last reported (in memory only at the forwarder, at most `most_offered`): the offered list is filled from the computers whose report says they take new accounts, and the computers list's `always_on` and `last_seen` are each computer's own report. A report the forwarder no longer answers (the computer's session ended, or the forwarder restarted and forgot them all) is kept at each computer for `report_held_ms` after it was last seen, so a forwarder restart neither blanks `last_seen` nor drops an always-on computer from the rule's counts (which would add a computer for nothing); past that the computer is no longer counted from its report. A computer has room (`has_room`) when it holds fewer accounts than its `accounts` limit and the volume of its accounts folder has `room_bytes` free above the floor its stores keep (its report's `storage.keep_free_bytes`; 0 for a fixed `bytes` budget): 1 GiB, a chosen number, not measured from old trillion, which had no such report.

host_kinds._what: Host kinds of the computers an account names (src/account/computers/copy_rule.rs). One row per account and computer, a list row in the account's sign-in rows (family `lists`), id `prefix` + account + `:` + computer id, value {revision, settings: {kind}}, changed by one compare-and-set on its revision. Each kind names the purposes its computers may hold (`allowed_purposes`). A computer with no row gets `existing_kind` when the account's computers row already names it (a migration default: every purpose, so running accounts keep today's behavior), and `new_kind` when it is new to the row (gauntlet default: sealed plus declared grants, so it answers for nothing until its row says otherwise). `computers::answer_allowed` is the one check: a computer named as answering for the first time (computers::apply) and a root sent to a computer (join.rs send-secrets-key) must be of a kind that allows `answer`, or it is refused with the HostKind cause. Rented hosts are `rented-host` (ciphertext only: sync and vote), since no rented host has attestation (L078 custody plan D1).
